title: The Painted Heavens of Another Country: an Ascoli decorator on Argentine ceilings
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Ascoli Piceno, birth in the travertine town
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia gives 29 May 1861 after Angelo de Gubernatis, Dizionario degli Artisti Italiani Viventi (1889). Spanish accounts give only 'Ascoli' with no province, and Ascoli Piceno is taken as the reading.
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of May 1861 a son is born at Ascoli Piceno, in the Marche, where the Tronto runs under travertine bridges and four centuries of masons and fresco painters have kept the churches in repair. The kingdom of Italy is two months old that spring. The boy will spend his working life on scaffolds, alone, months at a time, laying pigment above naves and stalls, and he will do almost none of it in this country. Ascoli gives him the trade, the name, and one architect fifteen years his senior, Francesco Tamburini, born in these same streets.
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Nazareno Orlandi', citing Angelo de Gubernatis, Dizionario degli Artisti Italiani Viventi (1889), p. 337
suggested_refs: Baptismal registers of the parishes of Ascoli Piceno for 1861, unconsulted; they would settle the street and the parish

stops.name: Ascoli Piceno, the drawing lessons at home
stops.date_confidence: year unrecorded; en.wikipedia states only that he studied design in his home town before entering the Academy at Florence, and this date marks a plausible schoolboy start rather than a documented one.
stops.campa: He is set to drawing in his own town first, in the way the Marche trains its craftsmen: the antique cast, the ruled perspective, ornament copied until the hand no longer needs the eye. Ascoli's churches are the classroom that costs nothing, their vaults carrying coffering and false architecture painted by men whose names the parish has forgotten. The lesson is a rate of work. One pair of hands covers a large surface slowly and comes back to it the next morning, and he will keep that rate for sixty years, most of them on another continent.
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Nazareno Orlandi' (studies design in his home town before Florence)
suggested_refs: Records of the drawing school of Ascoli Piceno in the 1870s, unconsulted

stops.name: Ascoli Piceno, the front of the Palazzo Ferri
stops.date_confidence: attested by it.wikipedia, which dates the collaboration with Domenico Ferri on the exterior of the Palazzo Ferri to 1880; no Italian archive has been consulted to confirm it.
stops.campa: His earliest dated work is on the outside of a building in his birthplace: the exterior decoration of the Palazzo Ferri, made in collaboration with Domenico Ferri. He is nineteen. It is also the only commission in Italy that any source attaches to his name; everything else from his Italian years is a prize, an exhibition, or an entry in a dictionary. The front faces an Ascoli street and stays there while its painter's whole later career happens six thousand miles away, on ceilings reachable only by ladder.
sources: it.wikipedia.org, 'Nazzareno Orlandi' (1880, Palazzo Ferri exterior, with Domenico Ferri)
suggested_refs: The Palazzo Ferri, Ascoli Piceno, and any surviving contract for its 1880 exterior decoration

stops.name: Florence, the Accademia di Belle Arti
stops.date_confidence: the year of entry is given by no source; only the graduation, 1885 in es.wikipedia, is dated. This date is a placeholder set four years before it.
stops.campa: At the Accademia di Belle Arti in Florence, in the old hospital of San Matteo on Via Ricasoli, he takes the academic course: drawing from the cast, then from the model, then from the fresco masters whose ceilings he will spend his life extending. The vocabulary he leaves with is quadratura and grisaille, painted architecture laid over flat plaster so that a room reads as a hall and a hall reads as open sky. No picture from his student years is recorded in any source. He leaves Florence with a method, and the method is what gets him hired.
suggested_refs: Matriculation registers of the Accademia di Belle Arti di Firenze, 1875-1885, unconsulted

stops.name: Italy, three years under arms
stops.date_confidence: no source names the years, the regiment or the garrison, nor whether the service precedes or interrupts the Academy; the pin falls back on his birthplace and the date is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Three years go to the Italian army. No source names the regiment, the garrison town, or the years, and none says whether the service comes before Florence or cuts into it. Only the fact and its consequence survive: he comes out of it painting soldiers. Battle pieces and military subjects become his line, the genre a twenty-year-old kingdom buys readily, and it is with these that he first shows in public. The painter of Argentine church vaults begins as a painter of Italian troops, and nothing in the record explains the turn.
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Nazareno Orlandi' (three years of military service, then military and battle subjects)
suggested_refs: Italian conscription registers (liste di leva) for the district of Ascoli Piceno, 1880s, unconsulted

stops.name: Perugia, first prize in the painting courses
stops.date_confidence: given by es.wikipedia alone, with the year but no month, competition name or jury; not corroborated by the Italian or English articles.
stops.campa: In Perugia he takes first prize in the painting courses, twenty-two years old and still short of his diploma. The city behind the prize is Perugino's, its walls carrying the soft distances that trained a young Raphael, and its academy hands out honors in a tradition it considers unbroken. He wins it two years before the Academy in Florence certifies him and six before any government sends for him. Only the year survives. Nothing on record says which picture won it, or who judged.
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Nazareno Orlandi' (First Prize, painting courses, Perugia, 1883)
suggested_refs: Prize records of the Accademia di Belle Arti Pietro Vannucci, Perugia, 1883, unconsulted

stops.name: Florence, the diploma
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia gives 1885 for the graduation; the English and Italian articles state the Florentine training without a year.
stops.campa: He graduates from the Accademia at twenty-four, with a diploma, a Perugian prize, and a trade that Italy has more of than it can employ. The peninsula in these years ships out its plasterers, mosaicists, stonecutters and fresco painters by the thousand, most of them contracted as labor and landed as labor. He leaves on the same tide four years later, under his own name and with a commission waiting, and every ceiling he paints afterwards stands outside Europe.
suggested_refs: Diploma registers of the Accademia di Belle Arti di Firenze for 1885, unconsulted

stops.name: Venice, the exhibition and the disputed third canvas
stops.date_confidence: the year and the first two titles are carried by both the English and Italian articles; the third title is contradicted between them and is left open.
stops.campa: He exhibits at Venice, showing 'Pro patria' and 'Mi ama, non mi ama?', and a third canvas whose title the sources will not agree on: 'Sana' in the English account, 'Pensieri profani' in the Italian. In the same season he works as an art critic, judging in print the pictures he competes against. No Italian exhibition lists him again for ten years. The canvases stop here, and what he paints afterwards is fixed to a building and known by the building's name.
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Nazareno Orlandi' ('Pro patria', 'Mi ama, non mi ama?', 'Sana'; art critic)
it.wikipedia.org, 'Nazzareno Orlandi' ('Pro patria', 'Mi ama, non mi ama?', 'Pensieri profani')
suggested_refs: The catalogue of the 1887 Venice exhibition, which would settle the third title

stops.name: Florence, the Dictionary of Living Italian Artists
stops.date_confidence: attested; the entry stands at p. 337 of the 1889 volume, printed at Florence by the successors of Le Monnier, and is the source later biographies cite for his birth data.
stops.campa: Angelo de Gubernatis prints his name at page 337 of the Dizionario degli Artisti Italiani Viventi, the register of living Italian artists issued at Florence by the successors of Le Monnier. The volume counts only the living, and it takes him at twenty-eight for a painter whose career will run its course on this peninsula. Every later biography draws his birth date from this page. In the same year, commissions begin to reach him from a government on the far side of the Atlantic.
sources: Angelo de Gubernatis, Dizionario degli Artisti Italiani Viventi: pittori, scultori, e architetti (Tipi dei Successori Le Monnier, 1889), p. 337
suggested_refs: The full text of de Gubernatis, p. 337, unread in this pass; it would give his Italian address and exhibition list as of 1889

segments.name: The Crossing and the Government Palace

stops.name: Genoa, the quay for the River Plate
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, not record: no source places Orlandi on any sailing or names a port, and the year itself is contested, es.wikipedia giving 1889 for the voyage and it.wikipedia 1899 for his settling in Buenos Aires.
stops.campa: The ships for the River Plate leave from Genoa, and Genoa carries more Italians to Argentina in these decades than any other harbor on the peninsula. No manifest reached names Orlandi on any of them, and no source gives his vessel or his day. What the sources give is the direction and the decade, and this quay is where the direction begins for almost everyone who takes it. Most who board go contracted for the wheat and the pampa, in gangs, with a season's work promised. He goes to paint ceilings for a government.
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Nazareno Orlandi' (1889 voyage to Buenos Aires)
suggested_refs: Passenger manifests of the Genoa lines to the River Plate, 1889-1899, unconsulted

stops.name: Buenos Aires, coming ashore at Retiro
stops.date_confidence: contested. es.wikipedia puts him in Buenos Aires in 1889; it.wikipedia and the city government's mural catalogue give 1899 for his settling there, with only 'commissions from the Argentine government from 1889' in between. Both readings are carried, neither adjudicated.
stops.campa: He comes ashore at Retiro, on the stretch of water where the state processes its Italians by the hundred thousand a year. The city he steps into is being cut open: boulevards driven through colonial blocks, a government palace half rebuilt, an economy a year from the crash of 1890. Two dates compete for this landing. Spanish sources put him on the quay in 1889; Italian and municipal ones give 1899 for his settling in the city. Ten years apart, and neither has been withdrawn.
sources: buenosaires.gob.ar, 'Murales de Buenos Aires', ficha avsantafe1860 (relocation given as 1899)
suggested_refs: Argentine immigration registers for 1889 and 1899, unconsulted; either would close the ten-year gap

stops.name: Casa Rosada, the summons and the silence
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia alone carries the Tamburini summons and the Casa de Gobierno commission; it.wikipedia says only that Argentine government commissions begin in 1889, and the Casa Rosada's own history does not mention Orlandi.
stops.campa: The Casa de Gobierno is being unified into one palace under Francesco Tamburini, the Ascoli architect who has directed the republic's public works since the middle of the decade, and the summons that brings Orlandi over is said to come from him and from the government of President Miguel Juarez Celman. The building's own record does not know it. The Casa Rosada's decorative history names Luigi De Servi for the Salon Blanco ceiling of 1910 and no one at all for 1889, and the Italian account says only this much of the year.
stops.quote: dal 1889 ricevette commissioni dal governo argentino
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Nazareno Orlandi' (Tamburini, Juarez Celman, Casa de Gobierno)
es.wikipedia.org, 'Casa Rosada' (Tamburini's unification from 1886; Luigi De Servi, Salon Blanco ceiling, 1910; silent on Orlandi)
suggested_refs: Argentine ministry of public works contracts for the Casa de Gobierno, 1886-1898, unconsulted

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the death of the architect
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia, 'Francisco Tamburini', gives his death in Buenos Aires in 1890; other listings give 1891. The contradiction is left standing.
stops.campa: Tamburini dies in Buenos Aires, forty-four years old, with the government palace, the Cordoba theatre and a great part of the republic's public architecture unfinished behind him. Orlandi has been in the country a year, brought over on the strength of one man's word, and now works without a patron in a city whose building boom is folding into the crisis of 1890. The year of the death is itself unsettled, 1890 in the Spanish record and 1891 in other listings. From here the painter takes his commissions where they come.
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Francisco Tamburini' (b. Ascoli Piceno 1846, d. Buenos Aires 1890)
suggested_refs: Tamburini's Buenos Aires death record, which would settle 1890 against 1891

segments.name: The Vaults of the New City

stops.name: Iglesia del Salvador, the Jesuit vaults on Callao
stops.date_confidence: carried by the Spanish and English articles and by the blog Historia del Mural Argentino; it.wikipedia's work list omits the church entirely and gives 1890 to another building. The church has no article of its own to cross-check.
stops.campa: On Callao, at Tucuman, the Jesuit church of El Salvador and the college that shares its wall take his brush: vaults, niches, painted architecture climbing on where the stone stops. It is devotional work, anonymous by design, a nave made to read taller and richer than it is, with no signature for the kneeling parishioner to find. Italian listings of his work leave the church out and give this year to another building instead, so the commission stands on the Spanish and English accounts alone.
suggested_refs: Jesuit provincial archives for the Colegio del Salvador, Buenos Aires, 1890, unconsulted

stops.name: Salon Dorado of La Prensa, the newspaper's ballroom
stops.date_confidence: the commission is attested and the year is not: it.wikipedia dates the ex-Palazzo della Stampa decoration to 1890, but the house at Av. de Mayo 575 (Carlos Agote and Alberto Gainza) was completed only in 1898. Spanish sources give no year at all.
stops.campa: The Salon Dorado of the Diario La Prensa on Avenida de Mayo is a newspaper's ballroom built to be mistaken for a French palace: gilt carving, mirrors, Gobelins tapestries, a ceiling of Athena among seven muses. He decorates it. The house later becomes the Casa de la Cultura and goes on holding the ceremonial life of a republic that no longer reads the paper which raised it. The room's own history names no decorator, and the single year offered for his work in it falls eight years before the walls were finished.
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Casa de la Cultura (Buenos Aires)' (completed 1898; Salon Dorado described, no decorator named)
Historia del Mural Argentino (blog), photograph captioned 'Mural de la Casa de Cultura de Nazareno Orlandi'
suggested_refs: La Prensa's own building accounts for the Salon Dorado, unconsulted; they would date the decoration

stops.name: Teatro Rivera Indarte, an attribution in Cordoba
stops.date_confidence: the attribution is undated in every source; this date is the theatre's inauguration, 26 April 1891, used as an anchor. es.wikipedia frames the claim with 'se le atribuye' and the theatre's own article credits the decoration to another man.
stops.campa: In Cordoba, Tamburini's theatre opens in April, completed by Giuseppe Franceschi after the architect's death, and tradition gives Orlandi a share in its decorative design. The Spanish source uses the verb that admits the doubt, se le atribuye, and pairs his name with a painter it calls Gonzaga Coni. The theatre's own account credits its facade reliefs, its attic quadriga and its Pompeian vault to Arturo Nembrini Gonzaga, and does not mention Orlandi. Both readings stand as they were found.
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Nazareno Orlandi' ('se le atribuye', with Tamburini and 'Gonzaga Coni')
es.wikipedia.org, 'Teatro del Libertador General San Martin' (Tamburini and Giuseppe Franceschi; decoration by Arturo Nembrini Gonzaga; inaugurated 26 April 1891)
suggested_refs: Cordoba provincial construction accounts for the Teatro Rivera Indarte, 1889-1891, unconsulted

stops.name: Chicago, the gold medal at the Columbian Exposition
stops.date_confidence: the medal is carried by the Spanish and English articles with the year only; no class, no jury and no exhibited work is named, and no exposition catalogue has been checked.
stops.campa: At the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago he takes a gold medal. The fair is the White City, acres of plaster neoclassicism raised on the lakeshore to argue that the New World can carry the old orders, and Argentina sends a pavilion of its own to make the same argument in produce and decorative art. What Orlandi showed there, whether it was painted in Italy or in Buenos Aires, and in what class the medal fell, no source consulted says. The medal is recorded; the work behind it is not.
suggested_refs: The official award lists of the World's Columbian Exposition, Chicago 1893, unconsulted

stops.name: Venice, honorable mention at the second Biennale
stops.date_confidence: given by the Spanish and English articles; one of them supplies the honorable mention. No Biennale catalogue entry has been checked, and the exhibited work is unnamed.
stops.campa: He returns to Venice for the second Biennale and comes away with an honorable mention, two years after the exhibition's founding, while it is still assembling the international standing it will keep for a century. A decorator working in Buenos Aires sends a picture back over the Atlantic to be judged in the city where he last showed, ten years before. His biographies carry the mention. No catalogue has been opened on it, and the picture itself goes unnamed.
suggested_refs: Catalogue of the second Esposizione Internazionale d'Arte della Citta di Venezia, 1897, unconsulted

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the year he stays
stops.date_confidence: 1899 is given independently by it.wikipedia and by the city government's mural catalogue; es.wikipedia gives 1890 for the decision to settle. The two-source reading is placed here and the Spanish one is not discarded.
stops.campa: Italian and municipal records agree on a year the Spanish ones do not: he settles in Buenos Aires in 1899, ten years after the first commissions came from its government. The decade between is thin enough to hold either story: crossings back and forth, or work already done in the city and only later called a residence. From here every commission on his list is Argentine, and no source records him crossing back to Italy in the fifty-three years he has left.
stops.quote: si stabili a Buenos Aires nel 1899
stops.quote_source: it.wikipedia.org, 'Nazzareno Orlandi' (rendered here without the accent, as it reached this account)
sources: buenosaires.gob.ar, 'Murales de Buenos Aires', ficha avsantafe1860
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires municipal padron entries for Orlandi in the 1890s, unconsulted

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Argentine citizenship
stops.date_confidence: the naturalization is attested by es.wikipedia and undated by every source reached, which name neither year nor court nor office; this date is a placeholder carrying no weight.
stops.campa: At some point in these decades he takes Argentine citizenship. No source reached gives the year, the court, or the office, and the fact survives without any of its paperwork. By the time he signs, he has spent years already on the ceilings of the country's churches, theatres, newspapers and ministries; the paper follows the work rather than opening it. Ascoli holds the record of his birth and Buenos Aires the record of everything he painted, and neither of them holds this one.
suggested_refs: Argentine naturalization registers, 1890s-1910s, unconsulted; the year and office are an open gap

stops.name: Biblioteca Nacional, Calle Mexico
stops.date_confidence: it.wikipedia attaches the old Biblioteca Nacional (Mexico 564, architect Carlos Morra) to his work list; the year given here is the building's inauguration, not a dated contract, and no Spanish source carries the commission at all.
stops.campa: The national library moves into a new house on Calle Mexico, built by Carlos Morra and opened in 1901, and Orlandi works in it. The building was raised for a lottery before the state gave it to the books, and it will hold them for eighty years before they go to a concrete hill in Recoleta. One Italian listing carries the commission. No Spanish source repeats it, and the library's own history of the house names its architect, its directors and its donors, and not him.
sources: it.wikipedia.org, 'Nazzareno Orlandi' (old Biblioteca Nacional, Mexico 564, arch. Carlos Morra, inaugurated 1901)
suggested_refs: Construction and decoration accounts of the Biblioteca Nacional building at Mexico 564, unconsulted

stops.name: Iglesia de San Telmo, the painted cupola
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Spanish and English articles and grouped with the same year by it.wikipedia; the church's own documentation has not been checked.
stops.campa: In the old parish of San Telmo the church of Nuestra Senora de Belen carries a cupola, and in 1903 he paints it. The barrio around it is by then a working district of conventillos and Italians, the wealthy having gone north after the fever years, and its colonial church acquires a painted heaven executed by a man from the Marche. He is forty-two. The work that reaches him now arrives when a dome is closed and left in bare plaster, and it no longer arrives from anyone wanting a picture with a title.
suggested_refs: Parish records of San Pedro Gonzalez Telmo for the 1903 cupola decoration, unconsulted

stops.name: Teatro La Comedia, the dome over the stalls
stops.date_confidence: attested by es.wikipedia and grouped with 1903 by it.wikipedia; the pin is the street address at Rodriguez Pena and is approximate, no located plan having been consulted.
stops.campa: The dome of the Teatro La Comedia takes the same year and the same treatment: a painted sky over an auditorium, figures foreshortened to be read from a seat a long way below. Theatres are the steadiest client a decorator has in this city, which builds them faster than it builds churches and expects each one to look like Europe. The dome is listed among his works with a year attached and nothing else. The building's own documentation is silent, and no photograph of the ceiling has been located.
suggested_refs: Photographic records of the Teatro La Comedia interior before its alterations, unconsulted

stops.name: Circolo Italiano, a ceiling for his own community
stops.date_confidence: it.wikipedia places the Circolo Italiano in the same 1903 group as San Telmo and La Comedia; no further description of the work survives in any source reached, and the pin is the club's address.
stops.campa: The Circolo Italiano, where the city's Italian bourgeoisie keeps its own society, is the third ceiling of that year. The commission stays inside one community: an Italian painter, an Italian membership, and a club that reads Italian decoration as the proof of having arrived. He has been in the country long enough to belong to the society that hires him, and it has been here long enough to afford him. The work carries a year and nothing else, not even a subject.
suggested_refs: Minutes and building records of the Circolo Italiano di Buenos Aires for 1903, unconsulted

stops.name: Teatro Municipal de Santa Fe, the ring of canvas
stops.date_confidence: the best-corroborated of all his Argentine commissions: es.wikipedia names him in his own article and again in the theatre's, independently. The theatre was built 1903-1905 and inaugurated 5 October 1905, so 1904 falls inside the campaign.
stops.campa: Up the Parana at Santa Fe, Augusto Plou is raising the city a theatre, begun in 1903 and opened in October 1905, and Orlandi paints the ring of canvas that runs around its interior. The theatre's own account names him, which no other building on his list does; everywhere else the painter names the room and the room says nothing back. The lienzo anular is still up there, over an audience that mostly does not look up, and it is the one work of his that can be checked against a source he did not supply.
stops.quote: en el interior se destaca un lienzo anular pintado por Nazareno Orlandi
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Teatro Municipal 1 de Mayo' (arch. Augusto Plou, built 1903-1905, inaugurated 5 October 1905, facade sculpture by Nicolas Gulli)
es.wikipedia.org, 'Nazareno Orlandi' (1904, dome of the Teatro Municipal de Santa Fe)
suggested_refs: Santa Fe municipal construction accounts for the theatre, 1903-1905, which would date and price the lienzo anular

stops.name: Catedral de Cordoba, sketches that will not date
stops.date_confidence: contradicted three ways: es.wikipedia dates a joint sketch campaign with Emilio Caraffa and Carlos Camilloni to 1904; the cathedral's own article dates Caraffa to 1900-1914 and Camilloni to the 1920s and never names Orlandi; it.wikipedia moves his cathedral work to 1916.
stops.campa: Spanish accounts put him in Cordoba preparing sketches for the cathedral's decoration alongside Emilio Caraffa and Carlos Camilloni. The cathedral's own chronology will not hold the three men in one year. Caraffa's frescoes and vault windows run from 1900 to 1914, Camilloni's campaign belongs to the 1920s with Manuel Cardenosa, and Orlandi appears nowhere in the building's list of hands. Italian listings move his cathedral work to 1916 instead. Three sources, three placements, and one nave that names none of them together.
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Nazareno Orlandi' (1904, with Caraffa and Camilloni)
es.wikipedia.org, 'Catedral de Cordoba (Argentina)' (Caraffa 1900-1914; Camilloni and Manuel Cardenosa in the 1920s; Orlandi not named)
suggested_refs: Cordoba cathedral chapter accounts for the interior decoration campaigns, unconsulted

stops.name: The old Bolsa de Comercio, since demolished
stops.date_confidence: undated; es.wikipedia gives the commission and states that the building on Calle San Lorenzo no longer exists. The pin falls back to the canonical Buenos Aires point because no located address survives, and this date is a placeholder.
stops.campa: He works the ceilings of the old Bolsa de Comercio on Calle San Lorenzo, a building that no longer stands. The exchange outgrew it, moved, and the house came down; whatever he painted there went with the plaster it was painted on. No photograph of the room has been located and no year attaches to the work. Of everything on his list this is the one that is wholly gone, painting and support together, which is the ordinary end of a trade whose work cannot be carried out of the room.
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Nazareno Orlandi' (ceilings of the old Bolsa de Comercio, Calle San Lorenzo, since disappeared)
suggested_refs: Photographs of the old Bolsa de Comercio interiors held by the Archivo General de la Nacion, unconsulted

stops.name: Teatro Colon, the mouth of the stage
stops.date_confidence: undated in every source; placed in the year before the theatre's inauguration on 25 May 1908, when work on the proscenium would have been in hand. es.wikipedia names the work and the collaborator; the theatre's own article names neither man.
stops.campa: At the mouth of the stage of the Teatro Colon, the arch that frames every performance the republic gives itself, he works with Domingo Fontana. The house has taken twenty years and three architects, begun under Tamburini and finished long after his death, and its decorative history recites a roster of Europeans with neither Orlandi's name nor Fontana's in it. His own entry names the work precisely; the building's account of itself names Marcel Jambon and, for the cupola of 1966, Raul Soldi. The silence runs one way only.
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Nazareno Orlandi' (boca del escenario, Teatro Colon, with Domingo Fontana)
it.wikipedia.org, 'Nazzareno Orlandi' (Teatro Colon in the work list)
es.wikipedia.org, 'Teatro Colon' (Marcel Jambon; Raul Soldi, 1966; silent on Orlandi and Fontana)
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires municipal accounts for the Teatro Colon's decorative contracts, 1905-1908, unconsulted

stops.name: Florence, honorary academician
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Spanish and English articles with the year only; the Accademia's own registers for 1910 have not been checked, and no source says whether he was present.
stops.campa: The Accademia di Belle Arti in Florence admits him as an honorary academician, twenty-five years after handing him a diploma and sending him out into a country with more decorators than ceilings. The honor goes to a man whose entire visible body of work is in another hemisphere, on walls no Florentine examiner will ever climb to. Whether he crosses the water to receive it, no source says. Nothing in the record establishes a single return voyage to Italy in the sixty-three years between his departure and his death.
suggested_refs: Registers of honorary academicians of the Accademia di Belle Arti di Firenze for 1910, unconsulted

stops.name: Plaza San Martin, the Italian pavilion of the Centenario
stops.date_confidence: carried by es.wikipedia alone, which says the Sociedad Italiana asked his collaboration in organizing events for the Italian pavilion; no exposition document has been consulted and the pavilion pin is approximate.
stops.campa: Argentina turns a hundred and stages an international exposition to prove it, and the Sociedad Italiana asks Orlandi to help organize the events of the Italian pavilion. It is the one moment the record shows him arranging rather than painting, standing for the community he came from inside the display the country is making of itself. Buenos Aires in 1910 holds more foreign-born residents than native ones, and the Italians are the largest body among them. He has lived in the city for two decades and still stands for the country he left.
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Nazareno Orlandi' (Sociedad Italiana, Italian pavilion, Exposicion Internacional del Centenario, 1910)
suggested_refs: Records of the Italian pavilion at the 1910 Exposicion Internacional del Centenario, unconsulted

stops.name: Palacio Paz, decoration for the newspaper's family
stops.date_confidence: it.wikipedia dates his Palacio Paz work to 1916, after the palace's 1902-1914 construction; the city's mural catalogue also credits him there. The palace's own article names sculptors and easel painters and no mural decorator, a silence rather than a denial.
stops.campa: The Palacio Paz on Plaza San Martin is the largest private residence ever built in Buenos Aires, raised between 1902 and 1914 for the family of Jose C. Paz, founder of the newspaper La Prensa, to designs by Louis-Marie Henri Sortais. Two years after its completion Orlandi decorates inside it, in rooms modeled on Versailles and the Loire, among French furniture and Carrara marble. He has now painted for the same family twice, in its newspaper's ballroom and in its house. The palace's list of artists names sculptors and no decorator.
sources: buenosaires.gob.ar, 'Murales de Buenos Aires', ficha avsantafe1860 (Palacio Paz among his works)

stops.name: Escuela Normal Mariano Acosta, ceilings for the teachers
stops.date_confidence: the commission is attested by es.wikipedia (undated) and by the blog Historia del Mural Argentino as the Colegio Mariano Acosta; the year comes from it.wikipedia, which groups it with the 1916 work.
stops.campa: The Escuela Normal Mariano Acosta trains the schoolteachers of a republic that has decided literacy is the instrument of nation-making, and Orlandi decorates it. The client is a state school rather than a palace, a club or a theatre, and its pupils will be posted out to the provinces to teach the children of immigrants to read Spanish. He paints the ceilings they train under. The Spanish sources give the commission no year at all; only the Italian listing puts it here.
sources: Historia del Mural Argentino (blog), as Colegio Mariano Acosta
suggested_refs: Argentine ministry of education building files for the Escuela Normal Mariano Acosta, unconsulted

stops.name: Catedral de Cordoba, the nave in the second dating
stops.date_confidence: it.wikipedia dates his work in the cathedral nave to 1916, against es.wikipedia's 1904 sketch campaign; both years are entered in this account and neither is confirmed by the cathedral's own record, which does not name him.
stops.campa: Italian listings put his work in the nave of the Cordoba cathedral in this year rather than in 1904, and the later date sits more easily beside the building's own account: Caraffa's campaign is closing, Camilloni's has not opened, and there is a decade of interior work still to be given out. The same listing groups the nave with the Palacio Paz and the Mariano Acosta school, so 1916 reads as a season of large contracts rather than a single job. Even so, nothing in the cathedral's own record names him in either year.
sources: it.wikipedia.org, 'Nazzareno Orlandi' (cathedral nave with Palacio Paz and Mariano Acosta, 1916)
suggested_refs: A comparison of the two datings against the cathedral's fabric accounts, unmade

stops.name: Gran Splendid, the allegory over the stalls
stops.date_confidence: attested and unusually well described: es.wikipedia's article on El Ateneo Grand Splendid gives the dimensions, the technique and the subject, and the city's mural catalogue carries the commission. The date is the theatre's opening in May 1919.
stops.campa: On Avenida Santa Fe, Max Glucksmann opens a theatre and picture palace by Pero and Torres Armengol, and Orlandi paints its dome: twenty meters by nineteen, in oil, an allegory of the peace that has just closed the war. A woman holds the center of it among clouds, flowers, doves, angels and nymphs, and a second woman carries a film projector, the new machine written into heaven in the year the house opens. Troiano Troiani supplies its sculpture. The building becomes a bookshop and the dome stays exactly where it is.
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'El Ateneo Grand Splendid' (Av. Santa Fe 1860; Pero y Torres Armengol; opened May 1919; dome 20 x 19 x 3.65 m, oil, allegory of peace, female figure, flowers, clouds, doves, angels, nymphs, second figure with a film projector)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, First Prize at the third Comunal exhibition
stops.date_confidence: attested by the exhibition's own printed Memoria (Talleres Casa Jacobo Peuser, 1928); the show opened 3 December 1927 and closed 12 February 1928, and the venue is not named in the sources reached, so the pin is the canonical Buenos Aires point.
stops.campa: At sixty-six he takes First Prize at the third Comunal exhibition of applied and industrial arts, opened in December by the municipal commission that runs the city's festivals and closed in February. The decorative arts are in their last confident decade; within a few years the plain wall wins the argument and the painted ceiling begins to read as period costume. His prize is recorded in the exhibition's own printed Memoria, which is also the volume later biographies cite for the date of his birth.
sources: Comision Municipal de Fiestas Populares, Memoria de la 3a Exposicion Comunal de Artes Aplicadas e Industriales: 1927-1928 (Talleres Casa Jacobo Peuser, 1928)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, death at ninety-one
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested by the Spanish, English and Italian articles alike and is consistent with a birth on 29 May 1861; no day and no month are given by any of them, and no obituary has been traced.
stops.campa: He dies in Buenos Aires in 1952, ninety-one years old, sixty-three years after the first Argentine commission and more than half a century after the Italian record stopped following him. Three encyclopedias carry the year and none of them a day. He has outlived the newspaper palace he decorated, the exchange whose ceilings he painted, the theatre that turned into a cinema, and the century that wanted painted skies at all. The name survives in his own entry and in one theatre article from Santa Fe.
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires civil death registers for 1952 and the Argentine press of that year, unconsulted

stops.name: Buenos Aires, a decorator without a grave
stops.date_confidence: no burial place is recorded in any source reached; the pin is the canonical Buenos Aires point and not a grave, and the date repeats the year of death for want of any later one.
stops.campa: No tomb, no funerary monument and no cemetery register has been found for him, and nothing has come afterwards either: no exhibition in his name, no biography, no restoration campaign called after its painter. His works are listed in the city's heritage pages and photographed every day by visitors to a bookshop who do not read the caption. The dome over Avenida Santa Fe carries no signature. Buenos Aires kept every ceiling he painted and no address for the man who painted them.
sources: Absence across es., en. and it.wikipedia, buenosaires.gob.ar heritage pages, and general web search
suggested_refs: Registers of the Chacarita and Recoleta cemeteries, and of the Italian mutual-aid societies' burial grounds, unconsulted
